title: Making and applying an image texture
content:
With the side of the Airline Chair unwrapped, you can paint a texture for it in a 2D image editor and put it on the model. In this part you'll export the UV layout as an image, use it as a guide to paint a quick test texture in Photoshop, connect that texture to a new material in Blender, and check how well the texture follows the UVs. You'll need the side you unwrapped in Part 3 and Photoshop or another 2D image editor. The video uses Blender 2.83 and Photoshop 2020.

Export the UV layout

  1. Choose Export UV Layout. 0:00 With the side in Edit Mode in the UV Editing workspace, choose UV → Export UV Layout in the UV Editor. The image is a guide to paint on in Photoshop or whichever 2D editor you use. On the right, tick All UVs; otherwise, select the UVs you want and leave it unticked.

  2. Set the size. 0:19 Set the size to 2048 × 2048. A 1024 × 1024 texture is called 1K, 2048 × 2048 is 2K and 4096 × 4096 is 4K. 4K is the best resolution for a production render 0:42; many companies and studios use 8K textures, but anything above 4K takes a lot longer to render. 2K keeps it simple.

  3. Export it. 1:02 Give the file a name (the video uses UV2) and click Export UV Layout. It makes an image file you can open in Photoshop 1:21.

Paint a texture in Photoshop

  1. Add a white background. 1:21 Open the image in Photoshop. Its background is transparent, and the UVs are on their own layer. Add a layer, move it to the bottom and fill it with white: Cmd+Delete fills it with the background color 1:45.

  2. Set the UV layer to Multiply. 1:50 Rename the UV layer (the video calls it uv) and set its blending mode to Multiply. Now anything you paint underneath it shows through 1:58.

  3. Paint on a texture layer. 2:02 Create another layer between them and call it texture. Paint on it: the video paints the side blue as a quick test 2:16. You can color outside the lines; Blender just ignores those pixels. To give other parts a different color, choose another color and paint over those UVs 2:35.

  4. Hide the UVs and save. 2:52 Turn off the uv layer, or the lines will be visible on the texture. Save the PSD file, then export a PNG: File → Export → Quick Export as PNG is the fastest way 3:00. Name it color rather than UV 3:14.

Apply the texture in Blender

  1. Add a material. 3:21 In Blender, open the Shading workspace: a real-time view of the textures at the top, and the Shader Editor for the material's nodes at the bottom 3:26. In the Material properties, click New. The new material is added to the object, and its Principled BSDF node appears in the Shader Editor 3:43.

  2. Add an Image Texture node. 3:50 In the Shader Editor, press Shift+A and choose Texture → Image Texture, and place it. Connect its Color output to the Base Color input of the Principled BSDF 4:06.

  3. Open the image. 4:06 Until it has an image, the node sends no color to the base color. Click Open on the node and choose your color PNG 4:13. The texture now shows on the side. In the same way, you could put any color information on the chair, such as a wood texture, using its UVs 4:22.

Check for stretching

  1. Test it with some type. 4:38 To see what stretched UVs would do, the video writes the word CHAIR in Photoshop on a new layer, over the side's UVs 4:43, checks it's on the UVs 5:07, and saves over color.png 5:13.

  2. Reload the image in Blender. 5:26 If the change doesn't show in Blender, reload the image: one way is to open the image again (Open Image) and choose the same file, which forces a reload 5:32. The type looks right on the model: it isn't stretched, a faithful reproduction of the lettering 5:43.

  3. See how the UVs place the pixels. 5:49 In the UV Editing workspace, the texture now shows behind the UVs. If you select some UVs and move them over a different part of the image, the model shows that part instead 5:58: the UVs locate the image's pixels on the polygons 6:11. Undo the move afterwards 6:17.

  4. Turn on the stretching display. 6:22 Press N in the UV Editor to open the Sidebar, and on its View tab, under Overlays, tick Stretching 6:35. It's hard to see with the texture behind it, so click the X beside the image's name to stop showing it 6:50: it's still the object's texture, it's just not previewed in the UV Editor.

  5. Read the colors. 6:56 All of it should be blue. Where UVs are stretched, other colors start to appear: the video scales a few faces' UVs up to show the distortion in color 7:15. Here there's only a little light blue, so the unwrap is a good one 7:27.

Wrap-up

You've exported the UV layout as a painting guide, painted a texture under it in Photoshop with the UV layer set to Multiply, and put the exported PNG on the chair with an Image Texture node. The stretching display shows how faithfully the texture follows the polygons. The only way to make it perfect is to cut more seams, so unwrapping is a balancing act between keeping stretching low and hiding seams as much as you can 7:34.
